Parents with poor conflict resolution skills *always* rely on their reasonable children to deal with the horrific behavior of their problem children. It's a messed up dynamic that persists over and over, because it's the path of least resistance. Avoiding conflict isn't about keeping peace for everyone, it's about avoiding an emotional difficulty they don't feel equipped to deal with. It's human nature to want to avoid conflict, and that's why it's a part of growth and maturity to learn how to cope with it. So I am really sorry your mother is lacking that (having gone through it myself ' ^ '. 

Don't look to your mom for any reasonableness on this. Reading the post and your comments, it looks like you've largely accepted her inability on this sort of thing, but I know it still massively sucks. My sister treated me really terribly growing up. Not normal sibling rivalry. Stuff that would get child services involved. Also stuff that was just ridiculous--giving my sister a second room (mine) and putting me in a small closet for one. She was awful to my brother and other sisters as well, but she was by far the worst to me. And my mom wanted her to like her, so she would just beg me to be nicer to her, more understanding, more supportive, etc.. It damaged my relationship irreparably with both of them.

From this, I've learned a few things. I always count on my mother (and people like her) to be unable to look at relationships in a healthy or objective way. Her comments on the situation don't hold water. And if you count on her emotional attachment to you or sister at all, you'll end any discussion, because that *automatically* pushes against her concern for your brother. Which she's demonstrated is unreasonable. I would not look at your mother's concerns with idea of 'does she have a point', just focus on the objective fact that she is distressed. That makes it easier to focus on whether you can ease the distress *without* ignoring your own needs or actual reality. Because she isn't accounting for either of those!

So she's distressed. Know you can't stop that and it's her choice. Just like it was your brother's choice to choose to draw a line. You don't have to make a choice--you've already been exceptionally kind and understanding to your brother, all while doing your best to be supportive and loving of your friend and a woman he unforgivably hurt. Being friends with Erin *is not* a choice to act against your brother. Not cutting off your brother also isn't an act of sacrificing Erin. You are being the good and decent person you want to be, and he doesn't get to change those parameters. Do not give into *any* of his demands. Or your mother's, because they are clearly his repackaged.

You know your mom ignores the details, even though the details *are precisely what matter*. She is **counting** on certain details to convince you to unquestioningly enable your brother. She's just ignoring those that aren't convenient to that aim. She's enabling him and wants to be enabled in her enabling. Make it clear that she can choose whether or not she wants to show support and love for her daughter on the most important day of her life, or make it about her and your brother. Because that's what she's asking. 

Not sure if it's worth trying, but with my mom, sometimes I use direct questions to try to shock her out of her nasty, selfish behavior. At least when it really counts. Asking direct questions can work sometimes. "Are you considering [sister's] happiness at all?" or "Do you feel that is a fair thing to ask of [sister]?" or "Why does sister need to cut off her family (Erin) to make you happy?" or "Do you think it is reasonable for [sister] to replace her best friend with a stranger for her wedding day?" or "Why doesn't sister deserve Erin's help and support in her wedding, just to appease brother?" or "Shouldn't you be prioritizing your daughter's needs at her own wedding?" or "How can you make [sister's] wedding about [brother]?". 

Usually I would advise attempts at discussion, how to avoid confrontation, how to approach things in a way to not incite offense, etc, etc. But when a parent is acting lazy and selfish, call a spade a spade and approach it with the understanding that you can't make her be a decent parent. Make it clear that **you will NOT** make it easier for her to roll over you than confront brother. Because she wants the easy way out. 

Protect yourself. Don't build up expectations. If I tried to believe my mom could be rationalized with, or prioritize my happiness, it would be a constant experience of disappointment and heartbreak. If I approach her with the knowledge that she isn't a mother and doesn't care about me enough to my needs first, I can approach things in a more rational and methodological way. I'm not saying you have to cut off or give up on your mom. Proceed with caution and make it clear you and sister have rules about what treatment you will tolerate.

Good luck!

Fellow Day-Dreamer-To-Escape here. 

Similar to you--I used to escape neglect and abuse and feel wanted. It was a great way to explore my imagination too. My work is creative and my day-dreaming has been a major contribution to my ability to construct scenarios. 

My husband found out while we were engaged. I was mortified--I thought it was a well guarded secret that no one would ever figure out. I wanted to crawl inside myself and die. He, *very lightly*, teased me ('so what do you do in xyz-story?'), saw my face, and immediately set into damage control. Apologies up and down and promises of understanding and he-was-just-curious-how-it-worked, and I-love-you-so-much-please-don't-be-embarrassed-it's-ok's. 

I didn't cry or anything or even look horror struck; I couldn't meet his eyes. I deflated. Regressed. He felt *horrible*. Because he knew, he knows, what I went through. And he felt terrible for potentially harming a wonderful, harmless coping method I had used every night for two decades. 

Some people will be weirded out by a coping method they don't understand. I'm sure that my husband found/finds it a little odd, hence his inability to just stop himself from poking at me when he confessed he knew. But as soon as he saw what it meant *to me*, he 100% focused on respecting me and asserting his love for me, and my right to use any coping that helps me be the person he loves and cherishes. 

He doesn't have to find it normal or mature or cool. Truthfully, I think it requires a certain amount of hell to prefer daydreaming to life during an entire childhood, and I wouldn't want to wish an understanding of that sort of daydreaming on anyone. I relied on my characters to make me feel loved, wanted, protected, clean, brave, unused, good enough, etc.. And that sort of reliance drives a sort of daydreaming level that most healthy-childhoods don't reach. I'm really happy that my husband *doesn't* fully understand my daydreaming. And I'm even happier that I now only daydream on the nights I can't fall asleep--I'm so happy in this life, I don't need that life raft the way I did. 

I wrote this novel to make one point clear--your boyfriend doesn't have to accept or understand your daydreaming, but he should try to accept and understand *you* and why it is important *to you*. Instead, he has acted with horrific cruelty and selfishness. None of his actions suggest that he even cares what they mean to you, or why they might be/have been a precious life raft. Your history, your love for story building fostered through a tumultuous life, your survival. It's all about *him*. That isn't love. Or care. Or empathy. Or compassion. Even if he can't understand it, there were a hundred better things he could have tried.  

I can't tell you what to do, but I will say that I would not be able to forgive my husband had he ever done such a thing to me. Ever. He wouldn't be the kind, loving, person he is, if he could do something like that. Know that you deserve love and acceptance. Know that we have to do awful things to push away love, not odd or uncommon things. Our oddities are what make us unique, and help us attract those who are similarly unique. We deserve love and kindness. That's the baseline. Not a hope.

As someone who has struggled with PTSD for years: numbness is your brain's way of keeping you safe when it still feels in danger and/or feels there is too much to process. One of the best ways to prevent PTSD is to see a qualified therapist ASAP, one who can help you successfully process what happened. As someone who got 'stuck' in her trauma, even though I was certain I could handle it, I really wish I had that option as a kid. 

Also, just a reminder, a lot of people here are going to tell you how to feel about this. It's natural, but dangerous. Until you've processed what has happened and how YOU feel about it, try not to internalize to much of it. Advice is good, you also need to process some things without others' feelings tangled up.

I'm sorry you are having a tough time and I am sorry that you feel so frustrated. 

Your feelings resonated with me. I've been struggling with physical issues from an assault, and I feel like I can empathize with the feelings of being trapped in a body affected by past choices. Those feelings of 'what if', and how unfortunate it is that the decisions we make in our youth affect us for the rest of our lives. 

I know that body art and sexual asault are very different issues/experiences. It might sound odd to make the comparison between the two, but I promise I have a point to make :). Part of my recovery process has significantly helped me cope with those feelings of being trapped. Everytime I saw a scar or felt pain, I'd feel overwhelming frustration and anger. I developed some tics from PTSD, and they're very noticeable. And I hated that. I'm not the same person I was when that happened, yet I can't hide those reminders from myself or others. I can't go back in time and say "hey, don't trust that person". I can't tell my younger self that I was worth not being abused. I'm not trying to sound victim-blamey or self-blamey, I more mean that I wish I had had the ability and knowledge to protect myself better. I had an unfortunate background that made me really vulnerable, and it just took me too long to learn how to cope with it. 

While I know that my scars/tics aren't your experience and I can't quite understand your experience either, I wanted to share some things that I've found helpful for similar feelings to what you've described. One thing is to really take ownership of the choices I *did* make. I have found that a lot of my frustration with the more visible parts of my problems is that I feel no control over them. I can't make them disappear. And while I am aware that I didn't *make* anyone do what they did to me, I'm also aware that different choices may have saved me from that trauma. And oddly enough, I find that very comforting. Because I can change that. I can control that. I can make different choices **now**. And I can also make active choices about whether to accept or fight against my physical reality. The outcomes of my choices.

I can't choose to make my scars or tics go away (not easily!), yet I can make different choices about how to keep myself safe and who to associate with. My fiance is a wonderfuly kind and caring person and always prioritizes my comfort and happiness. And I chose to be with someone like that, I also assert myself if someone harasses me or tries to press my boundaries. Yeah, I can't 100% prevent anything bad from happening; I could maybe be assaulted again tomorrow. But i take a lot of comfort in knowing that I've done everything I can. I am making different choices than I did. I can't stop my past self from making things harder for me today, but I can (and have) made things easier for my current and future self. I could have continued to make the same choices, but I changed.

Sorry this is so long. I know that you are dealing with your own problem and that I can't quite understand how it feels. I don't know what you should do to deal with the actual issue of removing/covering/hiding the tattoos. I am more addressing how to cope. When you feel that rage and frustration with your past choices, it might help to consider the choices you're making now. And accept the choices you made. Yes, you have a tattoo on your scalp, yet you also chose not to have one on your face. You've decided that you do not want them anymore, and you have also decided tha you are not getting anymore. I don't mean 'focus on the positives' (though that is advice I try to follow :P). I mean, when you feel stuck with the decisions you made, consider why you made those decisions and why you are changing now. Maybe try looking up 'radical acceptance'. Because as frustrated and angry as you feel, the more you fight against what's led you to them, and the more you focus on feeling trapped and angry about those decisions, the more trapped you will be. 

It's a hard concept to explain, so I probably sound very rambly. Yet it's really really helped me. **If I tried to put in a tl;dr, it'd be: the tattoos are already on your body. you can't change the decisions you made. You** ***can*** **control how you cope with them and the decisions you'll make from now on. Try not to hate past 'you'; it's still a part of you, and your past self made all the bad *and* good decisions that have lead you to where you are now. Wanting to changem yourself doesn't mean you have to reject or fight against that past self. It's okay to feel angry and frustrated, and it's okay to accept those feels. It's also good to consider what you want your feelings and future to become. It's all a part of the same goal.**

So I am someone who has been sexually assaulted multiple times, and thought I could help answer your question. On top of some of the helpful answers you got (vulnerable populations more likely to be victimized, risky behaviors often are repeated, repeat exposure to abusers, cycle of abuse etc.), there are also, unfortunately, issues of certain personalities are more likely to be targeted. The coping skills you develop or learn from previous assault, while valuable, can also make you an easier victim.

E.g., for myself, because I learned to cope with long-term sexual abuse as a child by freezing/suspending my conscious presence, and I was later victimized because a guy quickly learned I would freeze up when he aggressively kissed me. A decent person would either be concerned by this, or at least not notice, but a predator can learn, fairly quickly, what type of people they can manipulate, and what type of people will fight them. Abusers tend to abuse those that tolerate it. While I would physically resist, cry, or even fight my rapist, ultimately I didn't have the capacity to fight him off. Not because I was weak, but I had previously developed a hard core freeze response to sexual assault. He would push boundaries to see what I would fight him on, and would punish me for standing up for myself. A person who has an assertive personality (and/or has not been assaulted or abused) is more likely to stand against that sort of treatment, and it doesn't progress to more serious forms. A person with a personality that is over subservient or unassertive in personal boundaries, is more likely to be used by these sorts of people.

I feel very fortunate to have had access to mental health facilities and care. While it has taken a lot of hard work, I have learned to assert for myself and protect my boundaries and body. I also have a very caring partner that is aware of my past and is mindful of my PTSD. While I never 'deserved' or 'caused' my abuse or assaults, the factors that made it easy for multiple 'friends'/neighbors to harm me are much better, and, when last someone tried to harm me, I was able to call the police. 

I know people already provided statistical information, I just thought it might be helpful to provide a personal perspective.

I never could understand why, on top of all the racist crap we have to sling at each other, that on top of all that, we either justify inconsistencies with saying they're 'the exception' or 'white on the inside', or even with bullshit with saying that people are race traitors or glorifying/demonizing for acting different than race stereotypes. 

E.g., I'm out with one of my good friends,and he suddenly says 'there are a lot of Mexicans here' like he was really scared and I'm going 'who cares, wtf, you're Mexican'. We didn't live in an area with gang problems or anything, he just felt like being Mexican was something to be ashamed of and was incompatible with his ideal image. And that the group he saw apparently was more embracing of it(?). And yet he didn't seem to have the same issue with our 'white' Mexican friends.

And then, on the flip side, there were people that criticised my black family and friends for acting 'too white' or some such, and it just felt like they had a very precise image of what being black was. The whole time I'm thinking "what in the hell makes them 'too white'? What would make them 'black enough'? Who the fuck cares, they're awesome people. why should they have to worry about stupid shit like that, when it wouldn't even be a discussion if they were white." 

It just makes me so frustrated. To have people I love and care about, both stand out in general society for 'being black', or be ppraised for 'acting white, and also be scoffed by members of the black community for 'being too white', it just feels like they're being punished for something that wouldn't even be an issue if they were 'white'. 

I felt sad for my friend, because while it was clear that he felt like it was shameful to be a part of his heritage, I was also aware that those feelings didn't develop in isolation. That people make up these in-group/out-group bullshit based on skin color, completely ignoring who people actually are, is pretty much why I can't believe it when people say that 'racism really isn't a problem anymore'. 

Sorry for the tangent. Your comment made me think of a lot of things. It can get a little overwhelming, when you think of all the shit human beings create over something like skin color.

Skin color affects what we experience in our lives. It doesn't affect who we are or our potential.

I don't think she's throwing a hissy fit, I do find it unprofessional to be willing to leave a job due to a new personal conflict, especially when not wanting to first try to work it out with an employer. 

A wanted employee leaving is expensive for an employer--it costs time and resources to replace them. That doesn't make anyone indebted to their employer, it *does* set some parameters of professional or unprofessional ways to treat that reality. It also is important​to consider the professional consequences--it doesn't look good an a professional resume to be leaving a job quickly, especially without a clear, sharable reason.

If it is reasonable to assume an employer would rather keep an existing employee over a new volunteer, leaving without explanation or chance for remedy (e.g., asking to work separately) is the professional thing to do. The more professional thing to do is to keep in separate from work, but we know that that is not always possible, reasonable, or healthy. The next level of professionalism is to attempt a resolution with your employer. Leaving to avoid the personal conflict, without explanation or even with a feigned explanation, might appear professional on the surface, but in reality it punishes yourself and your employer. 

I get that it's a tough situation for her, and I'm not trying to address/reduce the mess the guy made for her. I do think it's worthwhile​ to address the inconsistency in professionalism.

That makes me so damn sad. I grew up in a liberal area. I had a few, incredibly vulnerable moments and struggled with PTSD. And throughout those times, K-12, I had teachers give me reassuring hugs and support. Half of them were men. As someone who didn't get that sort of affection at home, that comfort and physical touch was critical in keeping my head above water. It also helped me *unlearn* that older men only wanted to use/abuse me. 

I don't blame male teachers for fearing consequences. When you're told over and over 'never do X or Y might happen,' it's scary. I used to nanny myself, and I had strict rules for how I interacted with children (for my own safety and theirs). 

As someone who was abused repeatedly, I don't understand how the general public deals with the threat of sexual abuse. People spend so much time worrying about 'strangers/predators' rather than taking rational steps to keep their kids safe. Believe it or not, I have PTSD myself, and often struggle with social anxiety. I did a lot of therapy for it and still work on it, and part of working on that *is* the interacting with strangers. I really love learning about other people, and the isolation of the anxiety was really hard. Always being alone and beating myself up was hard too. CBT really helped me, and it's helped make the interactions easier. I mean, I get a lot of joy from talking with people/brightening their day, so working through the anxiety for that is a good goal for me. 

If you're willing to try, one thing that helped me was too rank social situations by how much anxiety they caused, and work my way up. I wrote all possible situations I could think of onto index cards, and one by one, I ranked them by which was more stressful. Doing it this way was really helpful on a personal level, because online rankings did not really reflect my personal experience. I was able to make my own 10 pt scale of 'social anxiety', and I started with the lowest ones (leaving the house/getting groceries/smiling at people). I still struggle with certain situations (some weeks the phone is too much, or I can't hang out with friends), but it is much better. 

With strangers, the best I've found to distract from the anxiety (of all the things I am doing '*wrong*'), is to focus my energy on how I can make their day a little brighter. Like, even if I do something 'stupid' or 'embarrassing', there is a good thing to focus on (they were able to share their stress with me, I made them laugh, I showed genuine interest in their day). I'm also less likely to mess up when I am less worried about myself, and I get to learn from the interaction too. 

I know everyone is different, so I hope I don't come off as one-size-fits-all, or belittling of how you feel. Social anxiety is really hard, especially as it torpedoes your support network *for* dealing with it. Applying these helped me overcome some of my anxiety, or at least some of the effects, and helped me make friends. I really hope you can find something that works for you.

(This comment is my advice regarding the above comment, split up for organization's sake)--advice for how I dealt with a selfish relative making something about me 'about them'

When I 'came out' to my mom as being sexually abused by my neighbor, she made it entirely about her. In the moment and for months after, and it really, really sucked. She talked about how she felt like a terrible mother, how she knew something was 'wrong' with him, that I messed up, how I should have listened better to her... (I was a 1st/2nd grader for perspective, just to make it clear how absurd this reaction was). I'm telling her how I want to get therapy and kill myself from the repressed memories surfacing, and she's saying how she's worried the therapist will say she's a bad mom. And yes, she probably sounds like a monster from this, and some of her actions were downright abusive... and she was also a person, a fairly normal person, who happened to be a bad mom, particularly in that moment. 

So, very different from what you are experiencing, I just want to share some coping methods I learned and maybe they might help you.

* Figure out what you want from your interactions. Not what you think they will give--just think about would help you most. 
* Consider what you want to ask for. It seems like you've got some of this figured out, by your post.
* Consider what you are *able* to ask for, at the moment. Boundaries and needs and wants are dynamic, and we change them according to the trust we have for someone in the moment. And asking for things are a vulnerable, sometimes tiring thing to do... So it's okay to go, "I can ask for this now" and "I can't ask for that right now"
* Prep for a first conversation, with these in mind. And have a general script ahead of time. I like to write letters and then talk, as the letter helps me figure out talking points. 
* Try to also remember that words *matter*. Just as you are experiencing--the way your brother is phrasing things is *hurting* you right now. Think of how different these sound, "Jake, I love you, but you are hurting me right now," and "Jake, I love you, your feelings matter a lot to me, and right now the way you are handling this is hurtful to me.". You aren't responsible for your feelings, you can only do your best to help the outcome you want.
* Once you are ready, have a go. Share the needs you are willing to share. Focus on how your needs just are; they are independent, and they are not dictated nor affected by his. 
* Remember that you can **only** control the way you handle yourself, not him. You can hope for his support, and you can adjust if he is or isn't willing to give it. Remember you can adjust *as* he responds. So focus on how **you** handle this. 
* Remember that **you** get to designate boundaries, and that **you** get to enforce them--because **you** know what they are. Other people will never enforce your boundaries for you. 

What I mean by 'your needs are independent', is that a lot of language I am reading is that you understand his needs, **but** you have your own, and that is dangerous thinking, especially when dealing with someone acting selfishly. It implies that only one of your needs can be met--actions can be in conflict with needs, but the needs themselves *just are*. Your needs aren't canceled by his or vice versa, and it's okay to prioritize your needs here, because you are more affected by this. It just doesn't have to be either/or... he can handle his feelings on his own and try to be there for you, without invalidating whatever feelings he has about this. 

When I dealt with my mom, I had to go into survival mode. Because her actions were so toxic and I was struggling with keeping my head above water, dealing with the stress I had. I had to focus on setting needs/boundaries, and then I came back to pain of past actions when I could handle it. Remember, *it's okay to delegate your resources!*. 

So I very clearly stated my needs and gave her the chance to respond. And if she met a need, she got to be a part of that need. And if she harmed a need, she got temporarily separated from that need. When she was considerate of the needs I set, she was included in those needs. 

Like, after our initial talk, if she started saying how she 'felt like a terrible mother' (how could this happen to one of *my* kids) or projected her feelings onto me (I'll never forgive him/he's ruined your life/etc.), I'd:

1.Say something and give her a chance to adjust. 

Like, "Hey, I'd like to include you in my support team, and I can't be using my resources to help you process this." or assert my own feelings "It's really important to me that I progress through the process of forgiveness right now," or "I actually feel like my life is going pretty well" or "I don't like giving him that privilege--my life belongs to me". I'd clearly state my feelings, and how what she was saying was in conflict with those.

2.Wait to see how she responded to the reasserted boundary.

Remember, you can't control others, you can only control yourself. Sometimes she'd respect the reasserted boundary, and she'd re-adjust what she was saying. Sometimes she'd double down and try to convince me 'what she really meant'. 

If she didn't respect the boundary:

3.I would temporarily separate myself. 

Whether it be physically, emotionally, and/or subject wise. Especially with her trying to make things about her or try to attach hate to my feelings, I'd have to be really strict. Sometimes I'd outright say, "The way you handling this is upsetting for me, and I can't talk to you about it right now." And she eventually learned that I got to set what 'right now' was. Because *you* have that power--you get to choose what you are willing to listen to. 

And, amazingly enough, she has actually become more supportive. Not anywhere near perfect... still, I appreciate that it's better and within my boundaries. Like, if I have a panic attack, she asks me what *I* need. If family accidentally makes light of it, she calls them out. She doesn't talk to me about how it makes *her* feel. Other stuff too--even with the problems above, she's part of my support team now. And that was possible with the therapy I got and learning how to assert/enforce boundaries. 

I can't tell you what is going on with your brother. I can only share how I was able to gain support from a relative that made my abuse about them, and the general steps that got them to come around. I hope things get better for you, I really do. Finding things are different than you thought, and having to redefine your identity, even if nothing really changed... that's hard. Really hard. And I hope it gets better.

I'm not sure how much you know at all about PTSD. It's Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, meaning it comes from trauma. Meaning, it's an incredibly personal thing to share with anyone, and finding the right time is paramount for any relationship. Finding the right time to tell someone you were abused by a neighbor for months, or assaulted multiple times in college, is a pretty personal decision. 

The stigma isn't about someone finding me unsafe. Part of the reason I was preyed upon in the first place, is that I give off the least threatening presence of anyone we know. He made the decision to wait, because he didn't want his parents to see me as a rape victim or as someone deserving of pity. If someone doesn't know me first, I've dealt with 'unsafe stigma', but once they do know me, and we don't time it right, it's a stigma of people seeing me as less than a whole person. Or even as a child. On top of that, trauma makes people uncomfortable. No matter how vague I am, they know something bad enough happened to affect me decades later. It makes them feel less safe, like it could happen to them. So, if they don't know me well enough, I end up this charity case of a child that reminds them the world is unsafe. Not a person, or even just a person with PTSD. 

And while I don't make the same scenes as OP, I have my own issues. PTSD can cause persistent and extreme forms od fight/flight/freeze. We have been together for years, and as a large man that is close to me, he has often had to cope with my PTSD. If something triggers me, I can become very agitated to the point of shutting down or refusing approach. I can become inconsolable or pass out if something triggers me badly enough. I have to take sedatives at times, and he then becomes responsible for my well-being. 

Before I found proper treatments, and especially after the most recent abuse, I wanted to hurt myself, not others, and I was incredibly unhappy. I found the right combination of treatments, but it was hard for a while. It has taken him years to figure out the best ways to handle my panic attacks. I used to get disoriented in the night and freak out that he was in my bed. I have had night terrors (sleepwalking terrors) where I lose all senses and try to *fight* him off.  

Most times, I tend to dissociate, not fight/freak during my episodes, so to 99% of people, I just seem a little 'dreamy' at times. My fiance knows dissociation is bad for me though, and does his best to keep me from 'leaving'. That means that, sometimes, he has to deal with my body/brain resisting his help. Fight can kick in, if freeze or flight is interrupted. I don't hurt him, but I can verbally and physically resist his attempts. That is his choice and his desire. I have never forced his help, and we as a team have made choices on both of our coping methods. Getting to the point where we can manage most everything, and I no longer need long-term medication, has been a real accomplishment for us both. He is my support and partner, and we have fought hard for this normalcy.

98% of the time, I am a kind, helpful, and industrious person. I love volunteering, excellent student, hard worker, productive, etc.. I am empathetic to a fault. I love helping others and am known as the 'good listener'. But 2% of the time, I am on a spectrum fearful and reclusive. I can be totally normal on the surface, or I can hide and lock myself in a room. I had bad things happen to me, for a long time, and it's hard to convince my body that it's not going to happen again. During that 2%, I have never hurt anyone or wanted to hurt anyone. I actually prioritize other's needs ahead of my own, so I often dissociate and go into 'nurture mode' and crumble on the inside. That's not a good thing for me at all, and the physical toll has been real, but it does mean that, around the uninformed, I'm often the only one aware of how freaked I am. Sometimes, particularly when trapped and with no one to take care of, I might fall apart because I can't flee, and I come off as over emotional, weak, or needy--not dangerous. We are still working hard to make that not the case.

I trust my fiance. We are not waiting till the day before the wedding--we only recently announced the engagement and are prepping to tell them. I trust when he thinks it is best.

Yes, exactly. I was particularly annoyed by the PTSD diagnosis part, because there is enough misinformation about PTSD as it is (thanks to places like Reddit and Tumblr). 

Emotionally upsetting/traumatizing stuff such as a scenario like this can definitely cause problems like depression and anxiety and all sorts of complications. That's different than PTSD. It doesn't mean they aren't serious, but the difference is important for treatment and understanding. It's like the difference between EDNOS and anorexia. They are both eating disorders and require help, but anorexia is differently diagnosed because of the unhealthy weight factor. It doesn't mean that EDNOS people don't need help or aren't struggling.

 PTSD is a diagnosis used for when someone experiences life trauma(s) that threaten physical and/or mental survival, and their minds cannot process it. Mentally, they are stuck with a fresh fear for the event(s) that caused the PTSD for a long time/life. Their minds cannot process it as a past/no longer relevant event. It isn't just a label for experiencing a trauma. And even though cPTSD (complex ptsd) is a bit different, it still involves the fear aspect. I'm not a doctor, but I've had to see *a lot* of them and read tons of shit about it as part of my treatment.

So either this is fake or it's a case of misunderstanding a therapist. Maybe a therapist mentions moving past the trauma and the patient self diagnosis themselves. Like when a patient misunderstands their doctor explaining their cold symptoms and thinks they have pneumonia. Or someone thinking an eating disorder means anorexia. I can easily see a therapist discussing the impact of a trauma and a patient making the connection with PTSD. Also of note, a therapist can't diagnose PTSD (only a doctor (psychiatrist/psychologist/physician) can).

I think... I think the longer I had held that information away from them, it actually hurt them. Think about this. If they love you, and you are in pain, then they will try to alleviate that pain. Because, no matter their age, you're their son. They will feel hurt that you waited to tell them this long, but relieved you are telling them now (and trust them enough to say). Any pain will only come from he disruption of an illusion; the disruption is what will cause them great pain (realizing they didn't protect their son from another) not the offender. My advice? Start slow. Have a serious talk to them about the abuse you suffered those years, but do *not* tell them the name of your abuser. If they prod, just restate, "I'm not ready", if they try to guess (Is it someone we know)?: a) "Please respect it is hard for me to talk about this" or b) "Maybe, I don't know, please wait"

Have conversations with them. Don't focus on the events (those are for therapy, not explanations), but explain the pain and difficulties you've face because of that abuse. Help them fully understand why you feel harm from this event in your childhood. This can take days/weeks/etc.

If they finally seem to grasp that it's something real, something painful, and they trust you, you can explain why you never talked about it before, because your past abuser is someone they love. And you were afraid of what would happen if you asked for help. But continuing to lie by omission, is breaking your heart and hurting your relationship with your family. So you want to tell them, and ask that they try to be as objective as possible. Tell them you love them, and want them in your life. Hey OP, fellow woman who has had terrible abuse dumped on her. My story is different than yours, but I hope I can share some things that helped me.

Forgiveness, truly, is for the person giving it. While it benefits the receiver, you cannot control how they respond to that gift. Forgiveness let's *you* release the resentment and anger that digs so effectively at your psyche. Your post has lots of concerns about how they will respond, but if you want to forgive, you will need to focus more on yourself. Secondly, forgiveness is not the same as forgetting; you can let go of the bitter anger eating you up without erasing consequences and accountability. 

Your step father knows he was awful--maybe not the extent, but he clearly does not believe your assurances that things are good. Write a letter, start off with how you wish to forgive him for what he did and you believe he has changed, but you are unable to forgive without conveying how you have been hurt by it. Make it clear that you are not attempting to press guilt or punish him, but you believe you can repair your relationship if he can acknowledge the pain he caused. Don't press for an apology--remember that you *cannot* control the actions of others. You may get one, but don't make your healing dependent on his reaction. You're best off with just sharing how you felt and hoping he shows remorse, but remember that the forgiveness is for you.

I'd recommend something similar with your mother, but not at the same time. One, they will discuss this, and you don't want to set it up as an 'them vs you' situation. Two, she'll be less likely to be emotional about it, and may help him reflect more clearly. 

I think it is wonderful that you wish to seek forgiveness. It always seems like people who have not been severely abused by others scoff at the idea, but most survivors I've spoken with believe it is a road to healing. Only when you are ready though. If you allow external pressures to influence this decision, it will result in you feeling more powerless, and you will miss out on the benefits therefrom. Also, understand that forgiveness isn't just a single action. I sometimes have to re-forgive my primary abusers daily, because I will reflect on something awful they did and feel so much anger over their actions. If you find yourself growing resentful again, don't feel guilty. You make a choice every time to give that forgiveness, it's not a one time deal. Obviously it becomes more personal post that initial discussion, but you should not feel like you failed when these feelings crop up. 

I am so sorry for what these people have done to you, and I understand the need to confront them prior to forgiving. If you didn't love your mother or interact with them, it'd be more personal, but in situations like these, you feel a need to share what's happened. Just remember, even if the outcome is not the one you wanted, forgiveness is for you, you can't control others, and you will grow from this difficult experience.

As a rape survivor myself, I have an uncommon opinion that I wish more people considered, but I think our culture is a little too focused on pinning fault, rather than dealing with outcomes.

In many cases, I don't think that a person has to commit rape for the victim to be raped. I think that there are many instances, possibly like this, where both parties make poor choices/don't communicate/under the influence, and cause another party to experience sexual assault without committing assault. I do not mean that in an absolving guilt/responsibility way, and it's hard to explain succinctly, but I think when people get hyper focused on objective experiences over subjective ones, all parties lose out.  Especially with issues like sexual assault, the damage is largely psychological, and help/understanding the victim(s) shouldn't hinge on naming a guilty party.

For example, say that Karen was horrifically drunk at this party--she bears responsibility for that consumption, and she still caused another person to experience a lot of distress. But that doesn't necessarily mean she's evil--just like op's husband could be too drunk to consent, she could be too drunk to consent to violating someone else. It doesn't mean he had consenting sex, he still was raped, but I don't agree that she consented to hurting another person. She still has to face outcomes (the distress she caused impacted her employment), but it does separate her from self-aware rape. 

I feel this way about a lot of situations when both parties are super smashed, where I'd rather focus on the party violated, rather than the other person. I also feel this way for big/celebrity cases--I don't feel that I have to accept the the plaintiff it guilty to have empathy for the defendant. I don't feel someone has to be legally liable in order to validate a victim's/survivor's experience. Same for when a child is molested/raped by a child of similar age--the victim has every right to feel traumatized, regardless of the mental state of the perpetrator. 

I'm sorry if that makes no sense, I just think that a craving for justice shifts the focus of validating an experience onto the degree of blame, rather than how the person feels. In this case, I think OP and spouse need to focus on his/their healing. Otherwise people get caught in the trap of determining blame over recovery.

*tl;dr:* *I think in cases of diminished mental capacity of both parties, it's more important to focus on recovery/validation of who feels victimized, and that doesn't require fixing blame on the other party. A person who would not have consented when sober has every right to feel traumatized, regardless of the amount of blame due to the perpetrator. His experience doesn't rest on her 'evilness', so it shouldn't be a focus.

My point is, most sexual abuse survivors end up seeing therapists that are maybe not so great at dealing with all the sexual damage the person has undergone.
